source_cards.back: A roundabout is a one-way circular intersection serving drivers, pedestrians, pedestrians with disabilities and bicyclists, in which entering traffic must yield to circulating traffic, and each approach carries a yield sign and may have yield line markings.

source_cards.front: When may you turn right on red, and to whom do you yield?
source_cards.back: After stopping on red you may turn right unless a sign prohibits it, and you must yield to all pedestrians and all vehicles while making that turn.

source_cards.front: When may you turn left on a red light?
source_cards.back: After stopping on red you may also turn left from a one-way street onto another one-way street whose traffic moves to the left, unless a sign prohibits that turn.

source_cards.front: How does a right turn on red differ from a left turn on red?
source_cards.back: After coming to a stop at a red light, you may turn right unless a sign prohibits it, while you may turn left on red from a one-way street into a one-way street where traffic moves to the left unless a sign prohibits that turn.

source_cards.front: What does a green light mean, and to whom do you yield?
source_cards.back: A green light means go straight or turn unless signs prohibit the turn, and you must yield to all pedestrians and vehicles already in the intersection.

source_cards.front: How does a green light differ from a green arrow?
source_cards.back: A green light allows going straight or turning unless signs prohibit, while a green arrow allows movement only in the arrow's direction.

source_cards.front: What do flashing red and flashing yellow signals mean?
source_cards.back: Flashing signals are sometimes used to warn of danger, a flashing red signal has the same meaning as a stop sign and a stop sign is also posted there, and a flashing yellow signal means proceed only with caution.

source_cards.front: How does a flashing red signal differ from a flashing yellow?
source_cards.back: A flashing red signal requires a full stop like a stop sign, while a flashing yellow signal allows you to proceed with caution.

source_cards.front: What do traffic signs tell you, and how do they carry meaning?
source_cards.back: Traffic signs tell you what actions you must take, warn you of possible hazards, and identify routes and locations, and their meaning is carried by color and shape as well as by words, letters, numbers and silhouettes.

source_cards.front: What does the color red on a sign mean?
source_cards.back: The color red on a sign means an action is prohibited, and red appears on signs of various shapes.

source_cards.front: What do yellow and orange signs mean, and what shapes do they use?
source_cards.back: Yellow on a sign warns of hazardous or dangerous conditions and almost always appears on a diamond-shaped sign, while orange warns of road work and appears on rectangular or diamond-shaped signs.

source_cards.front: What do black and white signs mean, and which colors mark guide signs?
source_cards.back: Black and white signs indicate a required action and are always rectangular, while green, blue and brown are used on guide and information signs, mostly rectangular as well.

source_cards.front: How do black and white signs differ from red signs?
source_cards.back: Black and white signs command an action and are always rectangular, while red signs prohibit an action and come in various shapes.

source_cards.front: What is a stop sign, and what must you do at one?
source_cards.back: A stop sign is an eight-sided white-on-red sign meaning other traffic has the right of way, so you must always come to a complete stop and yield to approaching traffic before proceeding.

source_cards.front: Where do you stop at a stop sign, and what if you cannot see traffic?
source_cards.back: At a stop sign you stop at the stop line, or before the marked or unmarked crosswalk if there is no stop line, and if you cannot see traffic from that first stop you move ahead slowly and stop again where you can see approaching traffic.

source_cards.front: What is a yield sign, and when must you stop at one?
source_cards.back: A yield sign is a triangular red and white sign meaning other traffic has the right of way, so be ready to stop, but you need to stop only when other traffic actually holds the right of way.

source_cards.front: How does a stop sign differ from a yield sign?
source_cards.back: A stop sign always demands a complete stop, while a yield sign demands a stop only when other traffic holds the right of way.

source_cards.front: At a stop sign without a stop line, where do you stop, and when twice?
source_cards.back: At a stop sign without a stop line you stop before the crosswalk, and when the view is blocked you creep forward and stop a second time where you can see traffic.

source_cards.front: What do do not pass signs mark?
source_cards.back: Do not pass signs are rectangular signs marking places on two- or three-lane roads where you must not pass another vehicle.

source_cards.front: What does a pass with care sign mark?
source_cards.back: A pass with care sign is a rectangular black and white sign marking the end of a no-passing zone.

source_cards.front: How does a Do Not Pass sign differ from a No Passing Zone pennant sign?
source_cards.back: A rectangular Do Not Pass sign marks locations on two-lane or three-lane roads where passing is forbidden, while a yellow and black pennant-shaped No Passing Zone sign on the left side of the road points to the start of a no-passing zone.

source_cards.front: What do speed limit signs show, and what must you obey?
source_cards.back: Speed limit signs are rectangular black and white signs that show the established maximum and minimum limits, which may apply only at certain times, under certain conditions or to certain kinds of vehicles, and you must drive neither faster than the maximum nor slower than the minimum.

source_cards.front: What does a reduced speed ahead sign tell you?
source_cards.back: A reduced speed ahead sign has the same color and shape as a speed limit sign and gives advance notice to begin slowing, and the new lower limit takes effect at the next speed limit sign.

source_cards.front: What do lane use control signs require?
source_cards.back: Lane use control signs are rectangular black and white signs showing that turns are required or unusual turns are permitted from specific lanes at an intersection, and you must move only in the direction shown for your lane.

source_cards.front: What do other alignment signs show?
source_cards.back: Other alignment signs are rectangular black and white signs showing where you must drive so traffic moves safely and smoothly.

source_cards.front: What do the other regulatory signs look like and restrict?
source_cards.back: The many other regulatory signs are all rectangular with black or red lettering on a white background, and they restrict people, vehicles, weights, vehicle types, parking and similar matters.

source_cards.front: How does a reduced speed ahead sign differ from the speed limit sign?
source_cards.back: A reduced speed ahead sign only tells you to start slowing, while the speed limit sign after it is where the lower limit actually takes effect.

source_cards.front: How does an exclusion sign differ from worded regulatory signs?
source_cards.back: An exclusion sign uses a red circle, with or without a diagonal slash, to prohibit a movement or activity, while other regulatory signs use black or red lettering on white to state restrictions in words.

source_cards.front: What do warning signs alert you to?
source_cards.back: Warning signs alert you to dangers that exist or may exist on or near the road, so be prepared to take safe and proper action when you see one.

source_cards.front: What do most warning signs look like, and which examples are pictured?
source_cards.back: Most warning signs are yellow diamonds carrying a black border and black symbols or words, and the examples pictured include divided highway, divided highway ends, hill, slippery when wet, pedestrian crossing, and lane ends or road narrows.

source_cards.front: What can the school sign mean, and what other warning sign is shown?
source_cards.back: One warning sign can mean either school crossing or school zone, and another warns of a traffic signal ahead.

source_cards.front: How do guide sign colors differ from warning sign colors?
source_cards.back: Guide and information signs in green, blue or brown locate places and services, while warning signs in yellow describe hazards.

source_cards.front: How does impatience affect stopping at signs and lights?
source_cards.back: Impatience shows when pressure from following vehicles and an empty cross street tempt a driver to make only a good try at stopping at a stop sign or red light, even for a right turn, until the stop becomes a mere slowing down.

source_cards.front: What does the ignorant driver fail to know, and whom do they blame?
source_cards.back: The ignorant driver does not know sign meanings, markings, right-of-way rules or safe procedures, turns from the wrong lane, drives too slowly from uncertainty, stops at the end of a freeway on-ramp or crosses markings that prohibit crossing, and usually blames other drivers.

source_cards.front: What must you obey while driving on a street or highway?
source_cards.back: You must obey every traffic law while driving on a street or highway, obey all lawful orders and directions of a police officer, and operate your vehicle as traffic signs, signals and pavement markings indicate.

source_cards.front: Which direction must you drive on a one-way roadway?
source_cards.back: On a one-way roadway you must drive only in the direction the posted signs indicate.

source_cards.front: How does left-half use differ on two-lane versus four-lane roads?
source_cards.back: You may use the left half of a two or three lane road to pass when no traffic is coming, while on a road with four or more lanes the left half is off limits unless signs direct otherwise.

source_cards.front: What do you do while waiting to turn left when the light turns green?
source_cards.back: When waiting to turn left at a red light and the light turns green, move slowly into the intersection with the wheels pointed straight ahead and turn only when the intersection is clear and it is safe.

source_cards.front: What should you watch for when turning?

source_cards.front: Where must you stop on a red light, and how long?
source_cards.back: On a red light you must stop at the stop line, or before entering the crosswalk if there is no stop line, or before entering the intersection if there is neither, and you must remain stopped until the signal turns green.

source_cards.front: How does a right turn on red differ from a left turn on red?
source_cards.back: After coming to a stop at a red light, you may turn right unless a sign prohibits it, while you may turn left on red from a one-way street into a one-way street where traffic moves to the left unless a sign prohibits that turn.

source_cards.front: What does a yellow light mean?
source_cards.back: A yellow light warns that red is about to appear, so you should avoid entering the intersection on yellow, and you must never enter the intersection after the red light is shown.

source_cards.front: What does a green light mean, and to whom do you yield?
source_cards.back: A green light means go straight or turn unless signs prohibit the turn, and you must yield to all pedestrians and vehicles already in the intersection.

source_cards.front: How does the yellow light rule differ from the red light rule?
source_cards.back: A yellow light warns that red is coming and you should avoid entering, while entering after the red light appears is flatly prohibited.

source_cards.front: How does yielding on green differ from yielding on a right turn on red?
source_cards.back: A green light requires yielding to pedestrians and vehicles already in the intersection, while a right turn on red requires yielding to all pedestrians and all vehicles.

source_cards.front: How does a green light differ from a green arrow?
source_cards.back: A green light allows going straight or turning unless signs prohibit, while a green arrow allows movement only in the arrow's direction.

source_cards.front: What do flashing red and flashing yellow signals mean?
source_cards.back: Flashing signals are sometimes used to warn of danger, a flashing red signal has the same meaning as a stop sign and a stop sign is also posted there, and a flashing yellow signal means proceed only with caution.

source_cards.front: What do flashing lights on a regular traffic signal mean?
source_cards.back: When a regular traffic signal shows flashing lights, the flashing red and flashing yellow carry the same meanings as the separate flashing signals.

source_cards.front: How does a flashing red signal differ from a flashing yellow?
source_cards.back: A flashing red signal requires a full stop like a stop sign, while a flashing yellow signal allows you to proceed with caution.

source_cards.front: What do lane control signals do, and where are they mounted?
source_cards.back: Lane control signals are mounted over the lane they govern and set the direction of travel in a lane that carries one direction at some times and the opposite direction at others.

source_cards.front: What do a green arrow and a steady yellow X lane signal mean?
source_cards.back: A green arrow lane control signal means you may use that lane, and a steady yellow X means you must move out of the lane because it is about to carry traffic in the opposite direction.

source_cards.front: What does a flashing yellow X lane signal mean?
source_cards.back: When the yellow X lane control signal is flashing, you may use that lane only while preparing to turn left.

source_cards.front: How does a red X lane signal differ from a red arrow?
source_cards.back: A red X lane control signal means the lane belongs to opposing traffic, while a red arrow means stop for that lane just as a red light would.

source_cards.front: What do red and yellow arrows mean?
source_cards.back: Lighted arrows are sometimes used to control turns from a specific lane, and a red arrow or a yellow arrow carries the same meaning as a red or yellow light for that lane.

source_cards.front: What does a green arrow mean?
source_cards.back: A green arrow has the same meaning as a green light for its lane, but you must turn or proceed only in the direction the arrow points.

source_cards.front: What are combination signals, and what must you do when a green arrow lights?
source_cards.back: Combination signals pair arrows with standard lights to control every lane, the colors and arrows keep their usual meanings, and when a green arrow is lighted you must move only in the direction it indicates.

source_cards.front: What do pedestrian signals control, and what do they display?
source_cards.back: Pedestrian signals control only pedestrian movements and use the lighted words WALK and DON'T WALK together with the symbols of a walking person and an upraised palm.

source_cards.front: Why are traffic signals used, and where are they installed?
source_cards.back: Traffic signals exist mainly to direct and regulate traffic, and they are installed at intersections and other places where the flow of traffic must be interrupted.

source_cards.front: When must you stop for a blind pedestrian?
source_cards.back: You must stop for any blind person in the roadway, identified by a white cane or a guide dog, regardless of the traffic signal or the traffic situation.

source_cards.front: What should a pedestrian do if the green has been showing a while?
source_cards.back: Never start across the street on a green light that has already been showing for some time; wait for the green on the next cycle.

source_cards.front: Where must pedestrians cross the street, and what should a pedestrian do when a green light has been showing for some time?
source_cards.back: A pedestrian must cross only within crosswalks rather than jaywalking, while a pedestrian facing a green light that has been showing for some time should wait for the green signal on the next cycle before starting across.

source_cards.front: Who do you yield to when the light turns green?
source_cards.back: When a light turns green you yield to pedestrians and to vehicles still caught in the intersection before you proceed.

source_cards.front: What do a solid yellow line and a flashing school bus mean for passing?
source_cards.back: You must not pass when a solid yellow line is in your lane, which is announced by a yellow no passing zone pennant on the left side of the road ahead, nor when a school bus on the same roadway has its flashing lights operating.

source_cards.front: What do you do when an emergency vehicle is right behind you, or stopped ahead?
source_cards.back: When an emergency vehicle is right behind you in heavy traffic, continue slowly until you can clear its way, and when you come upon a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights, slow or stop as the situation demands and, if it is safe, keep an empty lane between your vehicle and it.

source_cards.front: How does an approaching emergency vehicle differ from a stopped one?
source_cards.back: For an approaching emergency vehicle you pull out of its path and stop, while for a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights you slow or stop and leave an empty lane beside it when safe.

source_cards.front: What are pavement markings, and what do yellow centerlines separate?
source_cards.back: Pavement markings are lines, words or figures placed on the pavement with paint, reflectors or other markers, and yellow centerlines separate traffic moving in opposite directions.

source_cards.front: What do double solid yellow lines mean, and when may you cross them?
source_cards.back: Double solid yellow lines mark the center of a road where passing is prohibited in both directions, and you may cross them only to turn left into or out of an alley, private road or driveway.

source_cards.front: What is a no passing line, and when may you cross it?
source_cards.back: A no passing line is a single solid yellow line on a two-lane road marking a zone where passing is prohibited, and like the double yellow line it may be crossed only to turn left into or out of an alley, private road or driveway.

source_cards.front: How do yellow lines differ from white lines?
source_cards.back: Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, while white lines separate lanes moving in the same direction.

source_cards.front: What do white lines separate?
source_cards.back: White lines separate lanes of traffic moving in the same direction, and you are required to drive between them.

source_cards.front: When may you cross a single dashed white lane line?
source_cards.back: A single dashed white lane line may be crossed whenever you can do so safely.

source_cards.front: What does a single solid white line mean?
source_cards.back: A single solid white line warns that changing lanes there is hazardous, a wider line signals a greater hazard, and such a line may be crossed only in unusual circumstances and only with great care.

source_cards.front: What does a double solid white line mean?
source_cards.back: A double solid white line means that moving from lane to lane is prohibited, and you must not cross it.

source_cards.front: How does a single solid white line differ from a double solid white?
source_cards.back: A single solid white line may be crossed only in unusual circumstances with great care, while a double solid white line may never be crossed.

source_cards.front: What are obstruction markings?
source_cards.back: Obstruction markings are solid lines in the traffic lanes, yellow or white, that steer you around an obstruction in the road such as a bridge support.

source_cards.front: What is a two-way left turn lane, and what may it never be used for?
source_cards.back: Two-way left turn channelization markings combine solid and dashed yellow lines to mark a center lane that vehicles traveling in either direction may use only for left turns, and the lane must never be used for passing.

source_cards.front: What is a stop line?
source_cards.back: A stop line is a solid white line running across the lanes at an intersection or pedestrian crosswalk, and it shows exactly where to stop.

source_cards.front: How does a two-way left turn lane differ from plain double yellow?
source_cards.back: The two-way left turn lane is open to vehicles from both directions for left turns only, while double solid yellow lines without such a lane allow crossing only for a left turn into a driveway or alley.

source_cards.front: What do railroad crossing pavement markings consist of?
source_cards.back: Railroad crossing markings are white markings in the traffic lane before a crossing, consisting of a large X with two R letters, a solid yellow centerline running the whole distance to prevent passing, and a white stop line across the lane.

source_cards.front: What are traffic islands, and what do they do?
source_cards.back: Traffic islands come in many designs, from painted markings alone to combinations of curbing, paving or landscaping, and they are used to direct you into separate traffic lanes.

source_cards.front: How do railroad markings differ from red pavement markings?
source_cards.back: Railroad crossing pavement markings are white with a yellow no-passing centerline, while red pavement markings mean a roadway must not be entered at all.

source_cards.front: What controls traffic flow, and what are the three categories of devices?
source_cards.back: Traffic flow is controlled by pavement markings, traffic islands, signals and signs, and these devices fall into three categories, regulatory devices, warning devices, and guide and information signs.

source_cards.front: What do red pavement markings or reflectors mean?
source_cards.back: Red pavement markings or red reflectors mark a roadway that must not be entered or used.

source_cards.front: What are edge lines, and which colors go where?
source_cards.back: Edge lines are solid white or yellow lines along the edge of the roadway used as a safety guide, with white along the right edge and yellow allowed along the left edge of divided streets and highways.

source_cards.front: How do hazard flashers differ from turn signals in use?
source_cards.back: Hazard flashers indicate a vehicle in a hazardous roadway position and must not be used while moving. Signal every intended turn or lane change, including an intended turn while stopped at an intersection.

source_cards.front: How should you check behind before backing?

source_cards.front: How does entering a roundabout differ from exiting it?

source_cards.front: How much room must you give when passing a bicyclist?
source_cards.back: When passing a bicyclist keep at least three feet between the bicycle and your vehicle until safely past, remember the rider may be faster than you think, and avoid the common crash of passing and then slowing to turn right across the rider's path.

source_cards.front: What rules apply to bike lanes and right turns?
source_cards.back: Stay out of bike lanes, especially when turning right at an intersection, look for and yield to bicyclists when crossing a bike lane, do not pass a bicyclist if you are about to turn right, and train yourself to check for overtaking bicyclists at every right turn.

source_cards.front: Where must bicyclists ride on the road?
source_cards.back: Bicyclists must ride as near the right edge of the road as practicable but may move into the lane to prepare a left turn, pass another bicycle or avoid an obstacle at the edge, and they may legally ride along the left edge of a one-way road.

source_cards.front: Which bicycle crash comes from riders, and which from motorists?
source_cards.back: Wrong-way riding causes about a quarter of bicycle and car crashes, while passing a bicyclist and then turning right across the rider is the crash named for motorists.

source_cards.front: What do turning drivers and bicyclists often forget?
source_cards.back: When turning right, motorists and bicyclists alike often concentrate so hard on traffic from the left that they forget to check for pedestrians coming from the right.

source_cards.front: When may a slower bicyclist take the travel lane?
source_cards.back: A bicyclist slower than normal traffic rides as close to the right edge as practicable, may use the left edge on a one-way road, and may take the travel lane to turn left, avoid hazards, keep pace with traffic, or when the lane is too narrow to share safely with a motor vehicle.

source_cards.front: What should a bicyclist do before turning and near parked cars?
source_cards.back: Look behind and make sure it is clear before a left turn or a move into the travel lane, use proper hand signals for turning and stopping, and keep at least three feet from parked cars so a suddenly opened door cannot hit you while watching for cars pulling out.

source_cards.front: What are the two ways a bicyclist may turn left?
source_cards.back: A bicyclist may turn left like a motor vehicle, signaling, moving to the center of the lane when safe and completing the turn, or like a pedestrian by riding to the crosswalk, walking the bicycle across and riding on from there.

source_cards.back: A bicyclist may turn left from the center of the lane like a car, while the pedestrian-style option is to walk the bicycle across in the crosswalk.

source_cards.front: Where near intersections, crossings and bridges is passing banned?

source_cards.front: What yielding rules apply when changing lanes?

source_cards.front: How must you enter the road from a driveway?

source_cards.front: What do steady and flashing Don't Walk signals mean?

source_cards.front: What must you do when you see pedestrians near the road?
source_cards.back: As a driver you must slow and be ready to stop whenever you see people walking on or crossing the road or children near it, and the law requires you to sound the horn as necessary to warn any pedestrian on the roadway.

source_cards.front: What does the law prohibit regarding safety zones and stopped vehicles?
source_cards.back: The law prohibits driving through a pedestrian safety zone and prohibits passing a vehicle that has stopped to let a pedestrian cross.

source_cards.front: Where must you watch especially for children and pedestrians?
source_cards.back: Be especially watchful for children near schools, parks, playgrounds and residential areas, stop on the signal of any school crossing guard, and the law requires watching for pedestrians when turning at intersections and when entering or leaving driveways.

source_cards.front: How do duties toward blind pedestrians differ from other pedestrians?
source_cards.back: A blind pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog must be given a stop regardless of the signal, while other pedestrians are owed a slowdown, readiness to stop and a horn warning as needed.

source_cards.front: Which driver acts toward pedestrians are prohibited, and which is required?
source_cards.back: Driving through a pedestrian safety zone and passing a car stopped for a pedestrian are both prohibited by law, while sounding the horn to warn a pedestrian on the roadway is required by law.

source_cards.front: Where must pedestrians cross, and what do lines not guarantee?
source_cards.back: As a pedestrian cross only at crosswalks because jaywalking is illegal, obey all traffic laws and signals as the law requires, and watch for cars at all times because pavement lines and signals do not guarantee your safety.

source_cards.front: When does the law forbid a pedestrian from entering the street?
source_cards.back: The law prohibits entering the street or a crosswalk when vehicles are approaching close by, because they may not be able to stop, and you should look for turning vehicles before crossing and never run alongside or across a street.

source_cards.front: Where must pedestrians cross the street, and what should a pedestrian do when a green light has been showing for some time?
source_cards.back: A pedestrian must cross only within crosswalks rather than jaywalking, while a pedestrian facing a green light that has been showing for some time should wait for the green signal on the next cycle before starting across.

source_cards.front: Which side does a pedestrian walk on versus a bicyclist ride on?
source_cards.back: A pedestrian walks on the left side facing traffic, while a bicyclist rides on the right side with traffic.

source_cards.front: What do turning drivers and bicyclists often forget?
source_cards.back: When turning right, motorists and bicyclists alike often concentrate so hard on traffic from the left that they forget to check for pedestrians coming from the right.

source_cards.front: Where may bicycles be ridden on sidewalks?
source_cards.back: Bicycles may not be ridden on sidewalks in business districts, and elsewhere sidewalk riding is allowed only at ten miles per hour or less while always yielding to pedestrians.

source_cards.front: How does sidewalk riding differ in business districts?
source_cards.back: Sidewalk riding is forbidden in business districts, while elsewhere it is allowed at ten miles per hour or less with pedestrians given the right of way.

source_cards.front: Where do most fatal pedestrian crashes happen?
source_cards.back: Almost ninety percent of fatal pedestrian crashes happen in the roadway, more than half of them while crossing, and only slightly more than ten percent happen off the roadway.

source_cards.front: Why does pedestrian safety depend on both driver and pedestrian?
source_cards.back: The roadway is the domain of the motor vehicle, and a pedestrian who enters it has no physical protection, so safety depends entirely on the alertness and actions of both pedestrian and driver.

source_cards.front: How do the pedestrian death statistics break down?
source_cards.back: Pedestrians make up twenty percent of Hawaii traffic deaths, while almost half of pedestrian deaths are people under fifteen or over sixty-five.

source_cards.front: What are the two ways a bicyclist may turn left?
source_cards.back: A bicyclist may turn left like a motor vehicle, signaling, moving to the center of the lane when safe and completing the turn, or like a pedestrian by riding to the crosswalk, walking the bicycle across and riding on from there.

source_cards.front: How does a vehicle-style left turn differ from a pedestrian-style one?
source_cards.back: A bicyclist may turn left from the center of the lane like a car, while the pedestrian-style option is to walk the bicycle across in the crosswalk.

source_cards.front: What is a roundabout, and who yields on entry?
source_cards.back: A roundabout is a one-way circular intersection serving drivers, pedestrians, pedestrians with disabilities and bicyclists, in which entering traffic must yield to circulating traffic, and each approach carries a yield sign and may have yield line markings.

source_cards.front: How do you drive through a roundabout?

source_cards.front: How much room must you give when passing a bicyclist?
source_cards.back: When passing a bicyclist keep at least three feet between the bicycle and your vehicle until safely past, remember the rider may be faster than you think, and avoid the common crash of passing and then slowing to turn right across the rider's path.

source_cards.front: What rules apply to bike lanes and right turns?
source_cards.back: Stay out of bike lanes, especially when turning right at an intersection, look for and yield to bicyclists when crossing a bike lane, do not pass a bicyclist if you are about to turn right, and train yourself to check for overtaking bicyclists at every right turn.

source_cards.front: Why must you look before opening your car door?
source_cards.back: Look before opening your car door, because opening a door unexpectedly so as to endanger moving traffic, including bicyclists, is a traffic violation.

source_cards.front: How common are crashes from wrong-way bicycle riding?
source_cards.back: Riding against traffic is illegal, but many inexperienced bicyclists do it and this behavior causes about twenty-five percent of all bicycle and car crashes, so drivers should watch for wrong-way riders especially when turning.

source_cards.front: What legal status do bicycles have, and why stay alert for them?
source_cards.back: Bicycles are legally vehicles with all the rights and responsibilities of other vehicles, yet motorists must be extra alert for them because they are harder to see, may ride unpredictably, and show a wide range of riding ability.

source_cards.front: Where must bicyclists ride on the road?
source_cards.back: Bicyclists must ride as near the right edge of the road as practicable but may move into the lane to prepare a left turn, pass another bicycle or avoid an obstacle at the edge, and they may legally ride along the left edge of a one-way road.

source_cards.front: How much clearance should a motorist give a bicyclist when passing, and what rule applies to opening a vehicle door?
source_cards.back: A motorist passing a bicyclist should keep at least three feet of clearance until safely past, while opening a vehicle door unexpectedly in a way that creates a hazard for moving traffic or bicyclists is a traffic violation.

source_cards.front: Which bicycle crash comes from riders, and which from motorists?
source_cards.back: Wrong-way riding causes about a quarter of bicycle and car crashes, while passing a bicyclist and then turning right across the rider is the crash named for motorists.

source_cards.front: Which side does a pedestrian walk on versus a bicyclist ride on?
source_cards.back: A pedestrian walks on the left side facing traffic, while a bicyclist rides on the right side with traffic.

source_cards.front: Which laws must bicyclists obey, and which way should they ride?
source_cards.back: Bicyclists must obey all signs, signals and traffic regulations, which is the law and also earns respect for their place on the road, and they should always ride with traffic even for a short distance because motorists are not looking for fast bicycles coming from the wrong direction.

source_cards.front: What do turning drivers and bicyclists often forget?
source_cards.back: When turning right, motorists and bicyclists alike often concentrate so hard on traffic from the left that they forget to check for pedestrians coming from the right.

source_cards.front: When may a slower bicyclist take the travel lane?
source_cards.back: A bicyclist slower than normal traffic rides as close to the right edge as practicable, may use the left edge on a one-way road, and may take the travel lane to turn left, avoid hazards, keep pace with traffic, or when the lane is too narrow to share safely with a motor vehicle.

source_cards.front: How must bicyclists ride together, and what penalties apply?
source_cards.back: On the roadway bicyclists must ride single file, although they may ride two abreast on a bike lane or path wide enough not to impede traffic, and a bicyclist who breaks a traffic law faces the same penalties as a driver.

source_cards.front: What lane, lighting and passenger rules apply to bicyclists?
source_cards.back: Bicyclists must follow lane markings, leaving a right-turn-only lane when going straight, must have a headlight and rear reflector at night with a rear light, pedal reflectors and light clothing recommended, and must not carry passengers unless the bicycle is equipped for them.

source_cards.front: Where may bicycles be ridden on sidewalks?
source_cards.back: Bicycles may not be ridden on sidewalks in business districts, and elsewhere sidewalk riding is allowed only at ten miles per hour or less while always yielding to pedestrians.

source_cards.front: Where do bicycles ride on two-way versus one-way roads?
source_cards.back: Bicycles ride at the right edge of a two-way road, while on a one-way road they may ride along the left edge.

source_cards.front: Which bicycle night equipment is required, and which is recommended?
source_cards.back: A night-riding bicyclist must have a headlight and rear reflector, while a rear light, pedal reflectors and light clothing are only recommended.

source_cards.front: Why wear a helmet, and how should you ride?
source_cards.back: Wear a bicycle helmet every ride even where it is not legally required, because serious head injury does not require speed or distance, and be predictable by never swerving in and out of parked cars or traffic.

source_cards.front: What are the two ways a bicyclist may turn left?
source_cards.back: A bicyclist may turn left like a motor vehicle, signaling, moving to the center of the lane when safe and completing the turn, or like a pedestrian by riding to the crosswalk, walking the bicycle across and riding on from there.

source_cards.front: Why should a bicyclist not pass vehicles on the right?
source_cards.back: A bicyclist should not pass vehicles on the right, because drivers may not expect or see a rider there, and when traffic is stopped it is safer and more courteous to take a place in line.

source_cards.front: Why treat bicyclists with aloha?
source_cards.back: Treat bicyclists with aloha, since every bicycle on the road means one fewer car, less pollution and potentially one more open parking space at your destination.

source_cards.front: How does a vehicle-style left turn differ from a pedestrian-style one?
source_cards.back: A bicyclist may turn left from the center of the lane like a car, while the pedestrian-style option is to walk the bicycle across in the crosswalk.

source_cards.front: What causes most car and motorcycle crashes?
source_cards.back: Motorcycle riders are friends, relatives and neighbors, motorcycles are fuel and space efficient, but riders are more vulnerable to injury in a crash, and research shows that over two-thirds of car and motorcycle crashes result from a car driver turning in front of the motorcyclist.

source_cards.front: Where do car and motorcycle collisions most often happen?
source_cards.back: Intersections are the most likely places for car and motorcycle collisions, usually because the car driver does not see the motorcycle and turns into its path.

source_cards.front: How should you judge a motorcyclist's intention?
source_cards.back: A rider moves to one side of the lane to prepare for a turn or to avoid an unseen hazard, so never assume the rider's intention until the maneuver is unmistakably started, and remember that motorcycle turn signals do not cancel automatically and riders sometimes forget to switch them off.

source_cards.front: Where in the lane do motorcyclists ride, and why does it change?
source_cards.back: A motorcyclist's position in the lane changes with conditions, often riding in the left portion of the lane to see better and be more visible, but moving to the center or the right side to avoid traffic or be seen.

source_cards.front: Why might a motorcyclist suddenly shift position in the lane?
source_cards.back: Minor hazards such as potholes or railroad tracks that a car ignores can be major problems for a motorcycle, so the rider shifts position within the lane to gain distance from them, sometimes suddenly, and motorists must be alert for those quick changes.

source_cards.front: Why must you never share a lane with a motorcycle?
source_cards.back: Respect a motorcycle's space and position, because motorcycles are allowed the full width of a lane to maneuver, and never share a lane with a motorcyclist, since that restricts the rider's ability to avoid hazards.

source_cards.front: How far should you follow behind a motorcycle?
source_cards.back: Allow at least a two-second following distance behind a motorcycle so the rider has room to maneuver or stop, and increase the gap further because a motorcycle's speed and distance are hard to judge and sudden braking must be avoided.

source_cards.front: What should you do when a motorcycle passes you?
source_cards.back: Passing rules are similar for motorcycles, so a motorist being overtaken by a motorcycle keeps lane position and speed and lets the rider complete the pass and settle into proper lane position quickly.

source_cards.front: How should you pass a motorcycle?
source_cards.back: When passing a motorcycle give it a full lane, never crowd into its lane, and do not return to the original lane too soon, because that can force the rider to swerve right into traffic or off the road.

source_cards.front: How does being passed by a motorcycle differ from passing one?
source_cards.back: When a motorcycle passes you, you hold your lane and speed, while when you pass a motorcycle you give it a full lane and do not return early.

source_cards.front: How does the minimum motorcycle gap differ from the advised gap?
source_cards.back: Two seconds is the minimum gap behind a motorcycle, while an even larger gap is advised because the rider's speed and distance are hard to judge.

source_cards.front: What causes most skids, and when do you correct them?
source_cards.back: Most skids come from sudden changes of direction or speed, with excessive speed for road and traffic conditions the most common cause, so take extra care on wet, slippery or gravel-covered surfaces and correct a skid immediately and smoothly before control is lost.

source_cards.front: What is your first response when a skid starts?
source_cards.back: When a skid or control problem starts, stop or reduce whatever you were doing when it began, avoid the brakes and release them if braking started the skid, and ease off the accelerator, which may end the skid by itself.

source_cards.front: Which way do you steer out of a skid?
source_cards.back: To steer out of a skid, turn the wheel firmly but not sharply in the direction the rear of the vehicle is sliding, right for a skid to the right and left for a skid to the left, straighten as the skid stops, and if overcorrection starts a skid the other way, steer gently into that skid and repeat until you have control.

source_cards.back: In a skid you steer in the direction the rear is sliding and release the brakes, while off the pavement edge you keep straight, slow gently and steer back only at a safe speed.

source_cards.front: What is hydroplaning, and how does it start?
source_cards.back: Prolonged or heavy rain leaves a layer of water on the road, and at speeds up to thirty-five miles per hour tires with good highway tread wipe the surface like a windshield wiper, but at higher speeds the water cannot be cleared and the tires ride up on it like a surfboard, which is called hydroplaning.

source_cards.front: At what speeds does hydroplaning begin and become complete?
source_cards.back: Partial hydroplaning may begin at thirty-five miles per hour, it grows with speed and with the amount of water, and at fifty-five miles per hour in heavy rain the tires may lose all contact with the pavement, leaving you unable to brake, accelerate or steer.

source_cards.front: How can you prevent hydroplaning?
source_cards.back: To prevent hydroplaning keep good tread depth, because worn or bald tires hydroplane at lower speeds, keep tires at proper pressure, because under-inflated tires hydroplane at lower speeds, and reduce speed, because hydroplaning happens most at higher speeds.

source_cards.front: How does partial hydroplaning differ from complete loss of contact?
source_cards.back: Partial hydroplaning can begin at thirty-five miles per hour, while complete loss of tire contact can come at fifty-five miles per hour in heavy rain.

source_cards.front: How do the first drops of rain differ from prolonged rain?
source_cards.back: The first drops of rain make the road most slippery because of road oil, while prolonged rain creates the water layer that causes hydroplaning.

source_cards.front: What should you do when heavy rain cuts visibility?

source_cards.front: How should you drive in fog, and when must you stop?
source_cards.back: In fog, sharply reduce speed and use low beams, never high beams, whose reflection reduces your own vision and the approaching driver's, be ready for an emergency stop, and if you cannot see at least two car lengths, about forty feet, pull completely off the pavement, stop and turn on the hazard signals.

source_cards.front: Why use low beams rather than high beams in fog?
source_cards.back: Low beams are the rule in both fog and heavy rain, while high beams in fog reflect back and blind both you and the oncoming driver.

source_cards.front: When must you stop in fog versus in heavy rain?
source_cards.back: In fog you stop when you cannot see two car lengths, about forty feet, while in heavy rain you stop whenever you cannot see clearly even with the wipers on.

source_cards.front: When must a towing car have outside mirrors on both sides?
source_cards.back: If a trailer is large enough to block the view through the inside rear-view mirror, the towing car must have outside mirrors of proper size on both sides.

source_cards.front: When must a trailer have its own brakes and breakaway protection?
source_cards.back: A loaded trailer that weighs more than half the weight of the towing vehicle, or three thousand pounds or more, must have its own brakes and breakaway protection.

source_cards.front: May passengers ride in trailers?
source_cards.back: Passengers should not ride in trailers, and riding in a house trailer is prohibited.

source_cards.front: Where must trailer safety chains be attached?
source_cards.back: A trailer must have safety chains attached to the frame of the towing vehicle and to the trailer, never to a part of the hitch.

source_cards.front: What hitch should a towing vehicle use?
source_cards.back: The towing vehicle needs a hitch proper for the size and type of trailer, large trailers need special hitches, and a bumper hitch should never be relied on for any trailer.

source_cards.front: How much of a trailer's weight should rest on the hitch?
source_cards.back: A trailer load must be balanced so that about ten to fifteen percent of the trailer's weight rests on the hitch, because too much hitch weight makes steering difficult and too little makes the trailer fishtail, and the trailer must never be overloaded.

source_cards.front: What load, wheel and lamp requirements apply to trailers?
source_cards.back: The load must be held securely in place, and the trailer must have properly mounted and lubricated wheels covered by fenders or mud guards, good properly inflated tires, and tail, stop, turn signal and license plate lamps plus side marker lamps and reflectors where required.

source_cards.front: How do the trailer brake rule and the safety chain rule differ?
source_cards.back: A trailer needs its own brakes when it exceeds half the tow vehicle's weight or three thousand pounds, while every trailer regardless of weight needs safety chains fixed to the frames.

source_cards.front: What happens with too much versus too little hitch weight?
source_cards.back: Too much weight on the hitch makes the tow vehicle hard to steer, while too little makes the trailer fishtail, so ten to fifteen percent of the trailer weight is the target.

source_cards.front: How does the trailer mirror rule differ from the house trailer rule?
source_cards.back: A large trailer that blocks the inside mirror requires outside mirrors on both sides, while a house trailer may never carry passengers.

source_cards.front: What do large vehicles require from their drivers and from others?

source_cards.front: Which large vehicle limits apply to a car towing a trailer?
source_cards.back: Many car and small truck drivers tow trailers, and many of the limitations of large vehicles apply to a vehicle towing a trailer, especially a large one.
